To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

electrical brain stimulation of primary sensory areas (visual, auditory, somatosensory) is most likely to generate perceptual qualia when the spatially discrete, clustered neural activity most resembles natural sensory activation of the same area.
electrical brain stimulation is most effective when applied to clustered, spatially contiguous representations of sensory space.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the electrical activity of the brain and conscious experience.
the relationship between neural activity, sensory qualia, and the spatial structure of the cortex.
the relationship between neural activity, sensory perception, and the topographic organization of the brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
topographic organization of neural activity is critical to the perception of electrically evoked neural activity.
topography, or columnar microstructure, facilitates the detection and discrimination of discrete neural populations, which may then be used to infer perceptual qualia.
electrical brain stimulation is a powerful tool that, when used judiciously, can reveal a great deal about how neural activity generates conscious sensory experiences.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
electrical stimulation of the cortex can generate a wide range of perceptual experiences that can be quantitatively linked to the underlying neural activity.

we have demonstrated the ability to evoke a conscious percept in a human subject using electrical stimulation in the visual system, and that we have demonstrated a relationship between the location and the size of the evoked percept and the spatial location and the size, respectively, of the activated population of neurons.

electrical stimulation can be used to probe the relationship between neural activity, topography, and perceptual experience, but the relationship between neural selectivity and sensory experience is not yet fully understood.
